passage:
I've played in the college chess club since school, so I noticed Chetan the week he joined.
He plays fast. Really fast. "I just feel this move is right," he says, slapping a knight forward. In four games out of five, he's lost his queen by move fifteen.
It isn't that he's slow. He's brilliant at physics. But his gut here has almost nothing to go on. Mine was the same in my first year; it only got decent after hundreds of games where I lost, saw why straight away, and lost a little less.
Last Friday he asked, "Leela, why does your gut work and mine doesn't?" I showed him my notebook of blunders. He took a photo of the first page.
I don't know if he'll slow down. But he's started asking "why" after each loss.

qa.q: What does Chetan lose by move fifteen in four games out of five?
qa.a: His queen.

qa.q: Why does Chetan feel so sure about his fast moves?
qa.a: Chetan feels confident because the moves just feel right, and being brilliant at physics may make him expect his instincts to work here too, though he has little chess experience behind them.

qa.q: What could help Chetan build a gut he can trust?
qa.a: Playing many games, looking at each loss straight away to see why, and keeping a blunder notebook like Leela's.

qa.q: How does Leela see Chetan's fast play?
qa.a: Leela recognises that first year from personal experience, and knows his gut isn't foolish, just untrained.

grounding: A clubmate watches a new student trust his gut in chess, a game he barely knows, and lose often, while the narrator's own gut was built from hundreds of games with quick feedback.

passage:
First Saturday. On his first shift at the campus café, Karthik eyed the coffee grinder and said, "Feels about right." The shots came out sour. Sabina, the head barista, tasted one and winced. "You're guessing."
Second Saturday. Sabina made him pull ten shots, taste every one, and write down grind, time and taste in a little book. Sour, bitter, sour, better. Karthik groaned, but kept tasting.
Six weeks later. Karthik saw a shot running too fast and adjusted the grinder before Sabina said a word. She tasted it. "Good."
"It just felt wrong," he said. Then he laughed. "My gut's learning. Only took about four hundred shots."

qa.q: What did Karthik write down in his little book?
qa.a: Grind, time and taste for each shot.

qa.q: Why did 'feels about right' let Karthik down on his first shift?
qa.a: His gut had no coffee experience behind it, so the feeling of being right was really just a guess.

qa.q: Why did Sabina's method work?
qa.a: Tasting every shot and noting the settings gave quick, honest feedback again and again, which is what trains a gut feeling.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel when Karthik fixes a shot on his own?
qa.a: Pleased and a bit proud, since the weeks of tasting drills paid off. 🙂

grounding: Across several weeks, a student's untrained gut at the coffee machine is wrong until hundreds of shots with quick honest feedback make it reliable.

passage:
Bidisha, your great-uncle Imran was just like you at nineteen, sure of himself. That summer he came home from college and decided he could read the weather. "Nazia Apa, no rain today, I can feel it," he'd tell me, and hang the washing out. Three times that week it poured.
Old Rafiq, the boatman at the ghat, would look at the river and the clouds for one second and say, "Take it in by four." He was right nearly every time.
Imran asked him the secret. Rafiq laughed. "Forty years of looking at this sky every morning, and getting wet whenever I was wrong."
Imran wasn't foolish. His gut just hadn't been out in the rain enough times yet.
So when you say you 'just know' about your new course, ask yourself: how many times have I been wrong at this, and found out?

qa.q: What did Rafiq tell Imran was his secret?
qa.a: Forty years of looking at this sky every morning, and getting wet whenever he was wrong.

qa.q: Why did Imran feel so sure there would be no rain?
qa.a: At nineteen he trusted his feeling, but it wasn't built on experience, so it felt certain while being mostly wrong.

qa.q: What question does Nazia want Bidisha to ask about 'just knowing'?
qa.a: How many times have I been wrong at this and found out? If the answer is few, the gut needs checking.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have seen young Imran?
qa.a: Probably with amused patience, remembering that his own sky-reading came from getting wet many times.

grounding: An elder recalls her brother at nineteen trusting his untrained gut about the weather while a boatman's forty years of feedback made his read reliable.

passage:
I'm Yogesh, site supervisor for twenty years. Swati joined us as a junior engineer eighteen months ago.
Tuesday morning, the concrete truck was waiting to pour the third-floor slab. Swati walked the formwork, stopped halfway, and frowned. "Hold the pour. Something's off." She couldn't say what.
The truck driver grumbled. I didn't argue; I've seen that look on older engineers. She got down on her knees and checked the props one by one. Near the corner, one support had been set on a loose brick instead of a proper base plate.
Afterwards I asked her how she knew. "I didn't," she said. "It just looked different from the hundred slabs I've walked. So I checked."
Maybe it was the angle, maybe a shadow. I can't say for sure. But the pour went ahead an hour late, and safe.

qa.q: What was the corner support set on?
qa.a: A loose brick instead of a proper base plate.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling before she could explain it?
qa.a: Swati felt uneasy that something was off, because the formwork looked different from the hundred slabs she had walked.

qa.q: What did Swati do with the feeling that made it useful?
qa.a: She treated it as a cue to check, holding the pour and inspecting the props one by one, instead of ignoring it or acting on it blindly.

qa.q: How does Yogesh see Swati's hunch?
qa.a: Yogesh recognises the look from older engineers and trusts it enough to wait, while admitting to not knowing exactly what she noticed.

grounding: A supervisor watches a young woman engineer sense a problem from experience before she can name it, and use the feeling as a cue to check.

passage:
March. In her third week on the surgical ward, Rituparna noted Mr Mohit in bed two as "comfortable". An hour later, the senior nurse spotted what she hadn't: he had gone quiet and pale. Rituparna replayed it all evening at home.
November. Bed six, Divyansh, a college student two days after surgery. His readings were normal. But Rituparna paused at the foot of the bed. He was too still; he wasn't scrolling his phone the way he had yesterday. She couldn't have named it. She checked everything again, found one reading edging the wrong way, and called the doctor.
The next morning, the senior nurse asked what had made her look twice. Rituparna thought about it. "Hundreds of patients, I suppose. He just didn't look like someone getting better. So I checked instead of guessing."

qa.q: What had Divyansh stopped doing that he did the day before?
qa.a: Scrolling his phone.

qa.q: What did Rituparna feel at the foot of bed six?
qa.a: Rituparna felt uneasy that something was wrong, though the readings were normal and she couldn't yet name it; he didn't look like someone getting better.

qa.q: Why was checking again and calling the doctor the right use of her hunch?
qa.a: The feeling alone wasn't proof, so she used it as a cue to look closer, found a reading moving the wrong way, and brought in the right person.

qa.q: How might the senior nurse see Rituparna's growth since March?
qa.a: In March the senior nurse had to catch what she missed; by November she caught it herself, which would be very reassuring to see.

grounding: Over months, a young nurse builds a sense that something is wrong from hundreds of patients and learns to treat it as a cue to check.

passage:
Pradeep, before your first night route, let me tell you about Gauri. She joined my depot when I was the manager there, one of our youngest drivers, maybe twenty-four.
In her second year she was driving the ghat road one foggy night. Nothing on the dashboard. The engine sounded fine to any passenger. But she pulled into a lay-by and switched off. "Siddharth Sir," she told me on the phone, "it sounds a little wrong. I can't say how."
The mechanic came. A fan belt was fraying, about to go.
Later she said it was the hundreds of trips on that road; her ears knew what normal was. But she never just trusted the feeling. She always stopped and checked.
Your ears will learn too. Until then, and even after, when something feels wrong, you check.

qa.q: What did the mechanic find on Gauri's bus?
qa.a: A fan belt that was fraying, about to go.

qa.q: What did Gauri feel was wrong on the ghat road that night?
qa.a: Gauri felt uneasy because the engine sounded a little wrong, though nothing showed on the dashboard and she couldn't say how.

qa.q: What habit is Siddharth passing on to Pradeep?
qa.a: When something feels wrong, stop and check, both now and later, once experience has trained the ears.

qa.q: How might Gauri's passengers have felt if the belt had snapped on the ghat road?
qa.a: Frightened and stranded in fog on a steep road; her stop spared them that, even if the delay annoyed some.

grounding: A retired depot manager recalls a young woman driver who sensed an engine fault from hundreds of trips and treated the feeling as a cue to check.

passage:
In the small Accra office, the hiring panel had just finished its fourth interview of the day. Mr Boateng, who had run recruitment for fifteen years, closed his folder. "That one's a no. I can tell in five minutes."
Kwame, the team lead and newest on the panel, had noticed something. Two of Mr Boateng's "tell in five minutes" hires from last year were now among the best on the team; two others had left within months. Nobody had ever tracked which was which.
"I don't doubt your read," he said carefully. "But could we also score each candidate on the same five questions, and look back in a year?"
Rania from HR nodded. "We've never checked how our gut calls turned out."
Mr Boateng grunted, then picked up the score sheet.

qa.q: How many years had Mr Boateng run recruitment?
qa.a: Fifteen years.

qa.q: Why did Kwame speak 'carefully' to Mr Boateng?
qa.a: He respected the man's experience and didn't want to insult him, while still believing gut calls in hiring needed checking.

qa.q: What did Kwame suggest, and why does it suit hiring?
qa.a: Scoring every candidate on the same five questions and looking back in a year, because hiring gives slow, mixed feedback that experience alone doesn't sharpen.

qa.q: How might Mr Boateng feel about the score sheet?
qa.a: He may feel his skill is being doubted at first, but could also be curious to see how his calls actually turn out.

grounding: A team lead notices a veteran recruiter's confident gut calls have mixed results and asks for scored data alongside the gut.

passage:
At the Monday meeting of the finance team, Naveen tapped the whiteboard. "Trust me, the market turns up by Diwali. Twelve years I've done this; I can feel it."
Farhan, the senior analyst, had heard the same confidence last year, when the market went the other way. He didn't doubt that Naveen was sharp. But markets bounce around for a hundred reasons, and a forecast can be right by luck or wrong by luck; twelve years of that doesn't teach the way twelve years of fixing engines would.
After the meeting he opened a shared sheet. "Let's log every prediction the team makes, with a date and a reason, and see after a year how we did against a simple average."
Naveen raised an eyebrow. "You think my gut's wrong?"
"I think none of us know yet," Farhan said. "The sheet will tell us."

qa.q: By when did Naveen say the market would turn up?
qa.a: By Diwali.

qa.q: How does Farhan feel hearing Naveen's certainty about Diwali?
qa.a: Farhan feels doubtful but respectful; he doesn't question that Naveen is sharp, yet he heard the same confidence last year when the market went the other way.

qa.q: What does Farhan's shared sheet do that gut feeling can't?
qa.a: It records every prediction with a date and reason and compares the results with a simple average, giving the honest feedback the market itself doesn't.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel when Farhan says 'none of us know yet'?
qa.a: A bit challenged at first, but the reply includes Farhan too, so it may feel fair rather than personal.

grounding: A senior analyst notices a colleague's confident market forecasts in a noisy field and asks for logged predictions alongside gut feeling.

passage:
Subject: Our scholarship interviews

Hi Anand,

Something from yesterday's panel keeps bothering me. Three of our senior members said they could "just tell" which students would succeed. They were very sure, and they've done this for years.

But I went through the files from five years back. The students they were most excited about did no better, on average, than the ones they picked with doubts. Nobody had ever looked, so nobody knew.

It's not that they're poor judges. Guessing how a seventeen-year-old will do over five years is just noisy; you rarely find out, and when you do, luck is mixed in.

I'd like to propose we keep the interview but add a simple scoring sheet and a yearly check on how our picks did. Gut plus data, not gut alone.

Can we discuss on Thursday?

Tarun (Mr Chopra to the students, as they insist)

qa.q: How far back did Tarun look in the files?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: Why did the senior members feel so sure they could 'just tell'?
qa.a: Years of interviews gave the senior members a confident, proud sense of expertise, but nobody checked the results, so that confidence was never tested.

qa.q: What does Tarun propose, and why does it fit this kind of decision?
qa.a: Keeping interviews but adding a scoring sheet and a yearly check, because predicting students' futures gives slow, noisy feedback that gut alone can't learn from.

qa.q: How might the three senior members react to Tarun's proposal?
qa.a: Some might feel their judgement is being questioned, while others might welcome finally learning how their picks did.

grounding: A senior coordinator notices confident panel members whose picks never beat chance in a noisy field, and proposes data alongside gut feeling.

"The bloods came back normal, Binita."

qa.q: Which of Binita's choices made the hunch safe to follow?

passage:
Last quarter, reviewing a client's accounts, I felt something twitch before I'd properly read a single number. One supplier's invoices were too neat: round amounts, every one dated on a Friday. In three years of audits, real invoices had never looked like that to me.
I didn't write "fraud" in my notes. A hunch isn't evidence. So I pulled the delivery records and matched them, invoice by invoice. Four had no delivery behind them.
Then I took it to Nazia, who has audited for ten years longer than me. She went through it cold, without my theory, and reached the same place.
"Trust your gut, beti," my father always says. I've learned where it's worth trusting. A week later a friend asked whether her cousin's café idea "felt like a winner". I told her honestly: my gut knows ledgers, not cafés.
Shreya

qa.q: How many invoices had no delivery behind them?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What made Shreya's hunch twitch?
qa.a: The invoices looked too neat, round amounts all dated on Fridays, which didn't match three years of real invoices she had seen.

qa.q: How did Shreya turn the hunch into something reliable?
qa.a: She matched the invoices against delivery records and had Nazia review it cold, without her theory, before drawing any conclusion.

qa.q: How might the friend feel about Shreya's answer on the café?
qa.a: Maybe a little disappointed not to get a yes, but it's more honest than a confident guess from outside Shreya's field.

grounding: A young auditor trusts a trained hunch, tests it against records, has a senior colleague check it, and stays humble about a field she doesn't know.

passage:

Ritika, one of our junior engineers, flagged a relay cabinet at the junction today. "The hum's wrong," she said. The readings were within range. She has maintained over two hundred of these cabinets, so I listened.

At dusk, walking home from the fields, Vaibhav stopped dead by the old banyan tree. "Amma, there's a bhoot up there. I heard it whoosh."
Indu didn't laugh. She crouched beside him. "You heard a whoosh? That sounds scary. Shall we be detectives and look?"
They stood still. Whoosh. A dark shape swooped out of the branches.
"That's a bat," Indu said. "Bats wake up in the evening to catch insects. They're shy. They won't come to us."
Vaibhav held her hand tighter. "Detective bat-watchers?"
"Detective bat-watchers," she agreed. He counted three more bats all the way home.

qa.q: What swooped out of the banyan tree?
qa.a: A dark shape, which Indu said was a bat.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav stop dead by the tree?
qa.a: He heard a whoosh and imagined a bhoot, so he felt scared.

qa.q: Which of Indu's choices helped Vaibhav most?
qa.a: She took his fear seriously, made it a detective game, and gave a simple true explanation about bats instead of laughing or adding scary stories.

qa.q: What would change if Indu had said, 'Yes, bhoots live there, so hurry home'?
qa.a: Vaibhav would likely become more frightened of the tree and the dark, perhaps for a long time.

grounding: A village mother plays along with her son's fear of a ghost in a tree, checks it with him, and gently explains the bats.

passage:
The washing machine began its spin, rumbling like thunder in the little São Paulo apartment. Tomás, four, raced into the kitchen and hid behind his mother's legs. "Mamãe, the dragon's angry!"
Priscila knelt. "The dragon sounds loud today. Are you scared of it?"
Tomás nodded hard.
"Want to see the dragon's secret?" She lifted him up to the round window. "It's the drum spinning fast to squeeze out water. That's the roar."
Tomás watched a red sock fly past. "The dragon is eating my sock."
"The dragon gives it back," Priscila laughed. "Clean."
Later he told his aunt Jana, "It's just spinning. But I call it Dragon."

qa.q: What did Tomás see fly past in the round window?
qa.a: A red sock.

qa.q: Why did Tomás hide behind his mother's legs?
qa.a: The rumbling spin sounded like an angry dragon to him, and it frightened him.

qa.q: How did Priscila mix play with truth?
qa.a: She asked about his fear, let the dragon stay as a game, and showed him the spinning drum so he learned the real cause of the roar.

qa.q: How might Jana feel when Tomás explains the dragon?
qa.a: Charmed that he knows it's just spinning but still enjoys calling it Dragon. 😊

grounding: A mother plays along with her son's washing-machine dragon, checks his fear, and shows him the simple truth without mocking him.

In the clinic waiting room, Karthik, five, pressed against Asif's side. "Abbu, will the doctor's snake-thing hear my secrets?"
"The stethoscope? What secrets?"
"That I ate the biscuits."
Across the room a mother told her son, "Sit still or the doctor will give you ten injections." Karthik's eyes went huge.
Asif lowered his voice. "Nobody gets injections for fidgeting. The stethoscope only hears your heart going thump-thump. No secrets."
"Is it scary?"
"It's cold, like a spoon. That's all."
Karthik walked in holding Asif's finger, whispering, "Cold like a spoon."

qa.q: What was Karthik worried the stethoscope would do?
qa.a: Hear his secrets, like eating the biscuits, so he would be found out.

qa.q: How was Asif's approach different from the other parent's?
qa.a: He gave simple true facts, that it hears heartbeats and feels cold, instead of scaring with a made-up threat about injections.

qa.q: How might the boy across the room feel after his mother's warning?
qa.a: He might become more frightened of the doctor and of injections, making the visit harder.

grounding: In a clinic, a father checks his son's imaginative fear and gives simple true explanations instead of scaring him with made-up dangers.

Before the maths exam in the school hall, Aman took out his lucky blue pencil, the one with bite marks, and tapped the desk three times. Then three more, just in case.
Gopika, at the next desk, whispered, "You know a pencil can't do sums, right?"
"I know," Aman whispered back. "But last time I forgot it and got a C."
"Last time you didn't revise."
Aman went red. "Still. I feel better with it."
Sangeeta Ma'am, walking the rows, noticed the tapping. She didn't take the pencil. She stopped by his desk and said quietly, "Lucky pencil's fine. Your revision is what does the work." Aman nodded and started on question one.

qa.q: Why does Aman keep the pencil even though he knows it can't do sums?

qa.q: What did Sangeeta Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She let him keep the harmless pencil but reminded him that revision does the work, so the ritual doesn't replace effort.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Aman's ritual?
qa.a: Gopika finds it a bit silly, and points out that the missing revision, not the pencil, explains the C.

grounding: A boy taps his desk and carries a lucky pencil into an exam, half knowing it is illogical but feeling safer with it.

My brother Sahil is ten, and he walks to school like the pavement is lava. He hops over every crack. If he steps on one by mistake, he goes back and steps on it with the other foot, "to even it out."
On match days he wears the same green T-shirt, the one with the hole at the collar. Mummy has tried to wash it twice; he gets upset.
I'm Dolma, I'm thirteen, and I once asked him if he really thinks cracks matter. He shrugged. "Probably not. But what if?"
I can't see inside his head. He does seem calmer after hopping, and he still practises batting every evening. So I've stopped teasing him.

qa.q: What does Sahil wear on match days?
qa.a: The same green T-shirt, the one with the hole at the collar.

qa.q: What does Sahil's 'Probably not. But what if?' show about his thinking?
qa.a: He half knows cracks don't matter, but the ritual still feels safer, just in case.

qa.q: When is Sahil's habit harmless, and what would make it worth talking about?
qa.a: It's harmless while he still practises batting every evening; it would be worth a gentle talk if it made him skip practice or became very upsetting.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about the unwashed T-shirt?
qa.a: A bit frustrated about washing it, but she has seen how much it matters to him.

grounding: An older sibling describes a ten-year-old brother avoiding cracks and wearing a lucky shirt while half admitting it is not logical.

Sunday. Samir laid out his lucky shirt, the checked one he wore when he won the spelling bee. "Tomorrow's science test needs it," he told Francis on the phone.
Monday. After the night's rain, the shirt was still wet on the line. Samir's stomach dropped. He wore a plain one and kept touching his collar all morning, sure he'd mess up. Francis passed him a note: "It's just a shirt. You know the stuff."
Thursday. Results came back: eighteen out of twenty. Samir stared at the paper. "Maybe it was never the shirt," he told Francis. Then, after a pause: "I'm still wearing it for the final, though."

qa.q: What could Samir tell himself the next time the ritual isn't possible?

qa.q: How does Francis help Samir through Monday?
qa.a: Francis passes a note saying it's just a shirt and he knows the stuff, which is caring and down to earth.

Dear Sudha,

A small thing from Class 10 today made me smile, and then think.

Before the pre-board, I counted at least six students with lucky charms: a red thread, a keychain, one boy with a folded note from his grandmother in his pocket. Tanya refused to say her project was "nearly done" in case it jinxed it.

It's normal, I think. Most of them had also revised properly, and the charms seemed to calm their nerves.

The one I'm watching is Rishi. He told a friend he doesn't need to study for chemistry because he's got his "lucky pen". That's where it stops being harmless. I'll have a quiet word with him tomorrow, without mocking the pen.

Any thoughts?
Mohit

qa.a: She seemed to fear that saying good news out loud might jinx it, a small leftover worry from childhood magic.

qa.q: How does Mohit plan to handle Rishi, and why is that wise?
qa.a: A quiet word without mocking the pen, because the charm isn't the problem; skipping chemistry revision is.

qa.q: How might Sudha reply to Mohit's letter?
qa.a: Sudha might agree the charms are fine as comfort, and share ideas for getting Rishi to study without making him feel foolish.

grounding: A teacher notices teenagers with lucky charms and jinx fears, sees it as normal, and steps in only where a charm replaces studying.

Tanvir, you should've seen my under-sixteen girls before the final. Ruhi had to bounce the ball exactly seven times. Mehak wore her socks inside out. And nobody, nobody, was allowed to say "we'll win" in the dressing room.
I used to think I should stamp it out. Then I realised they'd all trained four days a week for months. The rituals weren't replacing the work. They were just a way to hold their nerves. So I let them be.
There was one thing I did stop. Juhi wanted to play on a sprained ankle because she'd "got her lucky band on, so it'll be fine." No band fixes an ankle. She sat out and iced it.
So: charms, fine. Charms instead of sense? That's where I step in. Damini's rule.

qa.q: How many times did Ruhi have to bounce the ball?
qa.a: Exactly seven times.

qa.q: What were the players feeling that the rituals helped with?
qa.a: Nerves before the final; the rituals gave them a sense of control and calm.

qa.q: When did Damini step in, and why?
qa.a: When Juhi wanted to play on a sprained ankle trusting her lucky band, because that ritual was leading to a harmful choice.

qa.q: How might Juhi have felt about sitting out?
qa.a: Probably disappointed and frustrated, but safer, and perhaps later grateful that her coach took the ankle seriously.

grounding: A coach describes teenage players' lucky rituals and jinx rules as harmless nerve-settlers, stepping in only when one leads to a harmful choice.

passage:
I teach evening maths at the community centre, and I've noticed something about Tushar this month.
He was picked for the district chess squad. I only know because his friend let it slip; Tushar went pale and said, "Don't say it out loud, it'll jinx it." He also touches the small brass elephant on his keyring before every test.
Most of that seems harmless. He studies hard, and the elephant seems to settle him.
But on Friday I saw the squad's travel form in his bag, still blank, due Monday. "I'll fill it when it's definite," he muttered. It already is definite.
I can't say for sure what he's afraid of. I'm Ganga, not a mind reader. So I just offered to sit with him while he filled it in, elephant on the table.

qa.a: The small brass elephant on his keyring.

qa.q: Why won't Tushar fill in the travel form yet?
qa.a: He seems afraid that treating the selection as real will jinx it, so leaving the form blank feels safer.

qa.q: Why is Ganga's offer a good response?
qa.a: It respects his charm, elephant on the table, while making sure the superstition doesn't make him miss the Monday deadline.

qa.q: How might Tushar's friend feel after letting the news slip?
qa.a: The friend may feel a bit guilty after seeing Tushar go pale, though the friend was only proud of him.

grounding: A teacher notices a teenager's lucky charm and fear of jinxing good news, and helps when the fear starts to delay a real task.
